criterion_notes.c1: Examines community public drinking water and wastewater infrastructure and service availability on the Crow Reservation (especially Crow Agency, Montana), including distribution/collection line replacement, school connections, installation of a bulk town water dispenser ('water salesman'), distribution pressure for housing, and flood-related wastewater service interruption.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, this clearly qualifies (yes): it discusses legal, administrative, regulatory, and jurisdictional factors affecting tribal water and wastewater infrastructure (BIA trust land right-of-way rules, Dawes Act land fractionation, lack of tribal eminent domain, TERO vs. state grant contracting rules, sovereign immunity waivers, lack of septic enforcement, lack of operator certification rules, and lack of tribal authority to create water districts). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, although several subsections address capital-grant contracting and construction procurement hurdles rather than direct household access rules, it still qualifies (yes) because it examines utility institutional/regulatory structure and cost-recovery rules (establishment of an independent tribal utility authority versus state-law water districts with taxing authority to fund utility O&M), land tenure/fractionation rules governing water and wastewater line rights-of-way, and regulatory enforcement gaps. However, under both readings of Criterion 2 the paper is excluded for lacking empirical evidence (E05).
criterion_notes.c3: Published as a 'Communication' and explicitly referred to by the authors as 'the commentary', the article presents practitioner reflections ('lessons we have learned') from the AWWWA directors combined with a non-systematic literature and statutory overview. It contains no empirical research methodology, no primary data collection or qualitative/quantitative analytical protocol, and no systematic empirical synthesis (prior water-quality studies are only cited as background). Excluded as E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Narratively mentions community-level infrastructure and service availability/continuity facts in Crow Agency (replacement of the sewage lagoon, 75% of wastewater lines, and 50% of water lines; upgraded school connections; installation of a low-cost 'water salesman'; insufficient water pressure for newly built homes; and a two-week wastewater service shutdown during the 2011 flood), though only anecdotally rather than as systematically measured empirical outcomes.
criterion_notes.c5: While the setting (Crow Reservation / Crow Agency, Montana) and institutional challenges are described, there is no identifiable empirical study design, sampling frame, or structured empirical measurement of exposure and outcome.

evidence_quotes.quote: With this funding, (1) the inadequate, failing sewage lagoon has been replaced with a modern one; (2) 75% of old wastewater lines have been replaced; (3) new, upgraded water and wastewater connections to local schools have been installed; (4) about 50% of water lines have been replaced; (5) a “water salesman” was installed to sell town water at minimal cost to any community member; and (6) 19 broken ﬁre hydrants were replaced.
Each type of land ownership requires a different process to obtain a right of way (ROW) to lay water or wastewater lines.

Tribal budgets to operate and maintain water and wastewater systems cannot be supported through the mechanisms available to non-tribal communities, as tribes lack the legal authority to create a water district.
John T. Doyle outlined the challenges described in this article [54], and Margaret J. Eggers conducted the literature review and drafted the manuscript, with edits from John T. Doyle.
The founding sponsors had no role in the conception of the commentary, in the writing of the manuscript, and/or in the decision to publish this manuscript.

For instance, housing has been built where there is insufﬁcient water pressure in the distribution system to accommodate more homes, despite the expressed concerns of the AWWWA. The lift station serving the south end of Crow Agency was built in the ﬂood zone; it was so damaged in the 2011 ﬂood that wastewater service was shut down for a couple weeks, including to the Indian Health Service hospital.

raw_response.exposure: Legal, jurisdictional, and institutional rules affecting tribal water and wastewater utilities on the Crow Reservation (BIA trust land right-of-way approvals, allotted land fractionation, lack of tribal eminent domain, TERO vs. state grant procurement conflicts, sovereign immunity waivers, lack of tribal statutory authority to form taxing water districts for utility O&M, and gaps in septic enforcement and operator certification)
raw_response.outcome: Descriptive narrative of municipal water and wastewater infrastructure upgrades and service issues in Crow Agency (replacement of sewage lagoon, 75% of wastewater lines, and 50% of water lines; school connections; bulk water dispenser; insufficient water pressure for new housing; two-week wastewater shutdown during 2011 flood), without empirical outcome measurement
raw_response.population_and_sample: Crow Reservation (primarily Crow Agency, approx. 2,038 residents; ~7,900 tribal residents reservation-wide), Montana, USA; no empirical sample
raw_response.rationale: Although this paper discusses community drinking water and wastewater service infrastructure on the Crow Reservation (c1) and examines tribal/federal/state legal, tenure, and utility regulatory hurdles—including trust land fractionation for distribution line rights-of-way and tribal lack of statutory authority to form taxing water districts (c2)—it is published as a 'Communication' and explicitly described by the authors as 'the commentary', synthesized from a practitioner outline of lessons learned and a non-systematic literature review. Because it lacks any empirical study design, data collection protocol, primary empirical analysis, or systematic empirical synthesis (c3=no, c5=no), it must be excluded under code E05 (No empirical evidence) under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2.
raw_response.study_design: Non-empirical practitioner commentary / communication and narrative literature overview (no empirical study design)
